messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was twenty-two when the convoy was ambushed outside Kandahar. He was a gunner on the second Humvee, and when the first IED detonated, the noise didn't register as sound so much as a physical force that inverted his understanding of the world. The vehicle ahead erupted. He saw Rodriguez—who'd shown him pictures of his newborn daughter just that morning—thrown from the turret. The screaming started immediately, and Marco fired back at the tree line, his hands moving on muscle memory while his mind fractured into a thousand simultaneous moments: the smell of burning rubber and flesh, the weight of the gun, the impossible clarity of Rodriguez's face as it turned toward him one last time. When the medevac arrived, Marco was still firing. He had no memory of climbing down from the turret, no recollection of the medic wrapping the burns on his shoulder. What he did remember, with photographic precision, was the exact shade of dust hanging in the sunlight as the second round of fire came in, and the feeling of his own body moving through space as though it belonged to someone else.

Now, two years later, Marco worked as a financial analyst in downtown Denver, and the memories hadn't faded—they'd calcified into something fixed and immovable. The visceral details remained crystalline: the grain of the metal beneath his palms, the taste of copper and ash, the specific angle of the shadows across the compound wall. But the sequence was broken. He couldn't reconstruct the timeline of what happened when. Did the second volley come before or after Rodriguez fell? He'd replay the fragments obsessively, trying to reassemble them into a coherent narrative, but the pieces wouldn't fit. They appeared unbidden—a flash of Rodriguez's uniform, the sound of a car backfiring on the street below his office, the smell of diesel fuel—and then vanished just as suddenly, leaving Marco disoriented and gasping.

The clarity of those fragments had come to mean something terrible to him. They weren't just memories; they were evidence. The fact that he could see Rodriguez's face so perfectly, could feel the gun so acutely, meant that he had been fully present, fully complicit. He had been trained to fire. He had fired. And Rodriguez was dead. The more vivid the memory, the more inescapable the conclusion: Marco had acted in a way that no part of himself could reconcile. He wasn't the person who'd enlisted, who'd believed in something larger than himself. That person had died in the dust outside Kandahar, and what remained was someone who had killed, or failed to save, or both. The weight of that violated self pressed down on him constantly, and with it came a suffocating sense that there was no future worth having. What was the point of a career, of relationships, of any of it, when he was fundamentally compromised?

These beliefs had quietly reshaped his life. Because Marco had come to see himself as irredeemably changed, as someone whose actions had severed him from the world he'd known, he found himself withdrawing from the very people who might have grounded him. He stopped answering calls from his mother, stopped attending his sister's family dinners. When colleagues at work asked about his weekend, he gave one-word answers and turned back to his spreadsheets. Talking about what had happened, or even allowing others to know him as he was now, felt impossible—not just painful, but dangerous, as though honesty would confirm the verdict he'd already rendered on himself. He began avoiding the open plaza near his office building where the company sometimes held lunch gatherings, the sight of people sitting casually in the sun triggering a claustrophobic panic that felt like drowning in daylight. Anything that reminded him of loss—a news story about fallen soldiers, a photo of a young man in uniform on social media—sent him spiraling, and he'd find himself deleting apps, unfollowing people, shrinking his world to the narrow confines of his apartment and his desk.

The avoidance had calcified into routine. He took the same route to work each day, avoided the gym where his unit's memorial was posted, stopped going to the cemetery where Rodriguez was buried. Each restriction felt necessary, protective. But with each boundary he drew, he felt more alone, more convinced that the isolation was permanent and deserved. It was only when his manager pulled him aside in late October, noting that he'd missed three team meetings and seemed to be withdrawing from projects, that Marco realized something had to give. He sat in his car afterward, hands shaking, and for the first time in two years, he allowed himself to consider that the story he'd been telling himself—that he was permanently broken, that connection was impossible, that his future was foreclosed—might not be the only story available. That thought terrified him more than the memories themselves. But it was enough to make him search for a therapist.
